hook.support: You turn 18. Now there are bills, a bank, myGov and tax. Nobody shows you how. This course does. You’ll get it all sorted.
hook.core: Turning 18 comes with paperwork nobody warned you about. A myGov account. A bank app. A phone bill. A tax return. And lots of fake messages pretending to be all of them. This capstone gets your admin sorted, safely. You’ll finish with a system you can keep using.
hook.extend: Adult life runs on documents: government accounts, bank statements, bills and contracts. Each has its own layout and rules. And scammers copy them all. In this capstone, you’ll find, read and organise the real documents of adult life. You’ll also judge how well they inform you.

why.support: Sorting your admin saves money and stress. It keeps you safe from scams.
why.core: Missed bills cost late fees. Scams cost Australians billions. Knowing your admin protects your money and your identity.
why.extend: Managing official papers and online accounts is a key adult skill. Mistakes and scams can cost real money, and cause legal trouble.

articles.title: Get your admin sorted

body.support:
When you are an adult, you have **admin**. That means accounts and paperwork.

**1. myGov**
**myGov** is a government website. It links things like:
- Medicare (for health).
- the ATO (for tax).
- Centrelink (for payments).

Always type **my.gov.au** yourself. Don’t click links in texts or emails.

**2. Your bank**
- Check your **bank statement**. It shows money in and money out.
- Look for things you didn’t buy.
.
**3. Bills**
On every **bill**, find:
- how much you owe.
- the **due date**.
- how to pay.

Late bills can cost extra.

**4. Stay safe**
- Use a long password. Don’t share it.
- Turn on a second check, like a code.
- A **scam** is a trick to steal your money. If a message rushes you, stop and check.
body.core:
Adult life comes with admin: accounts to set up, documents to read, and bills to pay on time.

**1. myGov**
**myGov** is the Australian Government’s online account. You link services to it:
- **Medicare:** health cover and your Medicare card.
- **ATO:** tax returns and super.
- **Centrelink:** payments like Youth Allowance.

Go to **my.gov.au** by typing it yourself, or use the official app. Real government messages won’t ask you to send your password.

**2. Banking**
- Your **bank statement** lists every transaction: date, description, money out, money in, and balance.
- Check it each month for payments you don’t recognise.
- Know which bills come out by **direct debit**, so your account doesn’t go into the negative.
.
**3. Bills**
Bills have a similar layout. Find:
- the **account number** and billing period.
- the **amount due** and **due date**.
- **how to pay** (BPAY, card, direct debit).
- what happens if you pay late.
- how to contact them, or get help if you can’t pay.

**4. Security**
- Use a long **passphrase**, different for each account.
- Turn on **two-step verification**.
- Watch for **phishing**: messages pretending to be myGov, your bank or a delivery company. They often rush you or threaten you.
- If unsure, contact the organisation using details you find yourself, not ones in the message.
.
**5. A system.** Keep a list of your accounts, a calendar of due dates, and a safe place for documents.
body.extend:
Being independent means managing official texts and accounts. Each has its own layout, language and risks.

**Government services.** **myGov** links federal services such as **Medicare**, the **ATO** and **Centrelink**. Go there directly (my.gov.au or the official app), never through links in messages. Its inbox holds official letters, so check it often.

**Banking documents.** A **bank statement** lists each transaction: date, description, money out, money in and balance. Read it carefully. Does it match what you expected? Spot strange payments early. Track **direct debits**, since they can push your account below zero.

**Bills.** Most bills share a layout: account number, billing period, charges, amount due, due date, ways to pay and contact details. Many also include hardship information. That is support if you can’t pay. Compare two bills for similar services. You’ll see how clearly, or not, each one shows the key facts.

**Security.** In 2023, Australians reported losing **$2.74 billion** to scams. Protect yourself:
- a different **passphrase** for each account, and a password manager.
- **two-step verification** wherever you can.
- spot **phishing**: rushing, threats, odd links, requests for codes or passwords.
- check using contact details you find yourself.
- lock away or shred papers with personal details, to lower the risk of **identity theft**.

**A system.** Aim for a routine: an account list (with no passwords), a due-date calendar, and a safe place for documents.

caseStudies.title: $2.74 billion

body.support:
Each year, the government counts how much money Australians lose to **scams**.

In **2023**, Australians said they lost **$2.74 billion**. That is a huge amount.

More than **600,000** scams were reported.

Some scams pretend to be a bank or the government. Some offer fake jobs. Losses to fake job scams went up a lot.

The good news: losses were lower than the year before.

The lesson: stop and check before you click, pay or share your details.
body.core:
Each year, the **National Anti-Scam Centre** reports on scams in Australia.

Its report on **2023** found that Australians reported losing **$2.74 billion** to scams. That was about **13% less** than in 2022, but still enormous.

There were more than **601,000** reports.

Investment scams caused the biggest losses. Losses to **phishing** (fake messages that steal your details) and to **job scams** went up. Job scam losses rose by more than 150%.

Many scams pretend to be organisations you trust: banks, delivery companies and government services like myGov.

The best protection is simple: don’t click links in unexpected messages. Contact the organisation yourself, using details you find on its real website.
body.extend:
The **National Anti-Scam Centre**, part of the ACCC, publishes an annual **Targeting scams** report. It combines data from Scamwatch, ReportCyber, banks, IDCARE and ASIC.

For **2023**, combined reported losses were **$2.74 billion**, down about **13%** from 2022. Reports rose by about 18%, to more than **601,000**.

Investment scams caused the largest losses. But reported losses rose for **phishing**, payment redirection and **job scams**. Job scam losses rose by more than 150%.

Two patterns matter for young adults setting up their admin. First, scammers impersonate trusted organisations: banks, delivery companies and government services. Second, job scams target people looking for work.

These figures are reported losses. Many scams go unreported, so the true cost is likely higher.

The defences are procedural, not technical: access services directly, verify independently, never share codes, and slow down when a message creates urgency.

model.text:
**MY ACCOUNTS** (no passwords here)
- myGov: my.gov.au (Medicare, ATO linked)
- Bank: official app only
- Phone: account number on my bill
**DUE DATES**
- Phone: 15th of each month, $45, direct debit
- Gym: every 2nd Friday, $25, direct debit
**MY SCAM RULES**
1. Never click links in texts about my accounts.
2. Never share a code that’s sent to me.
3. If it rushes me, stop and check.
**MONTHLY CHECK:** read my bank statement for anything strange.
why: It lists the real way into each account, but no passwords.
Due dates include the amount and how it’s paid, so there are no surprises.
The rules are short enough to remember.

teacher.overview: A VM 3&4 capstone. Students access and organise the real documents of independent life: myGov and linked services (Medicare, ATO, Centrelink), bank statements, bills and digital security. They list their accounts (without passwords), read a real bill or statement, sort safe and scam messages, complete one real admin task, and create a personal admin cheat sheet. The case study is the National Anti-Scam Centre’s 2023 report: $2.74 billion in reported losses, with phishing and job scam losses rising.
prep: Collect sample bills and statements (redacted) for students without their own.
Remind students and families: never share passwords or codes, including with teachers.
Students should have done some Real-World Docs and On the Job courses first (this capstone requires two from each).
Know your wellbeing team’s contacts: money and housing stress can come up.

Statements: check monthly for unknown transactions; track direct debits.
Security: unique passphrases, two-step login, never share codes, verify independently.
A system: account list, due-date calendar, monthly check.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 account number (quote when calling); 2 billing period; 3 itemised charges (check each); 4 amount due; 5 due date (late fee); 6 payment options; 7 hardship or help.

**Sort:** scam — myGov suspension text with a fake domain; parcel fee with short link; caller asking for a code; $900-a-day job. Safe — letter seen after logging in to myGov yourself; notification inside the official bank app.

**Case study:** $2.74 billion reported lost in 2023, down about 13% from 2022; 601,000+ reports; phishing and job scam losses rose (job scams up more than 150%); real losses likely higher because many scams go unreported.
realityCheck: **Privacy first.** Students must never share passwords, codes, account numbers or tax file numbers in class. Redact documents.
**Not every student has accounts yet,** or a safe home situation for admin. The sample documents and “family member helping” option cover this.
**Money stress is real.** Bills and debt can be sensitive. Know your wellbeing referral pathway, and mention hardship programs.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students regularly find they’re paying for something they forgot about.
